title: How long does a 5% edge take?
hook: A new type leaves 5% more offspring. How long until it is half of everyone?

knows: selection favours variants that leave more offspring
doesNotKnow: that a small, steady edge compounds into a takeover
how many generations that takes, and that it looks like nothing for most of them

misconception: A 5% advantage either takes over in a few generations or makes no visible difference.
objective: The learner can explain that a steady edge multiplies the new type's ratio to the old one each generation, so in the toy model a 5% edge takes about 95 generations to go from 1% to half, stays rare for most of that time, and a doubled edge roughly halves the time.

claims.text: In the stage's toy model, a type that starts at 1% and leaves 5% more offspring than the old type each generation first reaches half the population at generation 95.
claims.source: Iterated p' = p(1+s)/(1+sp), s = 0.05, p0 = 0.01, in Demo.tsx (HALF[5]) and artifacts/scratch/w4life/nums.mjs: generation 94 = 49.8%, generation 95 = 51.0%. Closed form: odds grow by 1.05 per generation, ln 99 / ln 1.05 = 94.2. Matches the brief's check (95). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: first reaches half at generation 95 (94 = 49.8%, 95 = 51.0%).

claims.text: With the 5% edge, at generation 48 (about halfway to half) the new type is still only 9.5% of the population; at generation 10 it is 1.6%.
claims.source: Same recursion in Demo.tsx (TRAJ[5][48] = 0.0951, TRAJ[5][10] = 0.0162), re-run in node. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: generation 10 = 1.62%, generation 48 = 9.51%.

claims.text: In the same model a 10% edge reaches half in 49 generations and a 1% edge in 462: doubling the edge roughly halves the time.
claims.source: Demo.tsx HALF[10] = 49, HALF[1] = 462; artifacts/scratch/w4life/nums.mjs also gives 2% = 233. ln 99 / ln(1+s) is about (ln 99)/s for small s. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 10% edge 49, 2% edge 233, 1% edge 462.

claims.text: Each generation multiplies the ratio of new type to old type by 1 + s (1.05 for a 5% edge); going from 1 : 99 to 1 : 1 needs that ratio to grow 99-fold, about 95 steps of 1.05.
claims.source: From p' = p(1+s)/(1+sp): p'/(1-p') = (1+s) p/(1-p). Standard haploid selection recursion (Gillespie, Population Genetics: A Concise Guide, 2004, ch. 3). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: The model is a toy: a very large asexual population (no drift, no sex), a constant advantage, and no new mutations. It is labelled 'Toy: huge population, no sex' on the stage and in the question.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx; brief life #32 (company/domains/briefs/life.md). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

recall.question: A new variant has a small, steady advantage (a few percent more offspring per generation). Which describes its rise best?
options: It takes over within a few generations
It stays rare for a long time, then rises quickly to take over
It rises by the same amount every generation
A few percent is too small to matter
recall.why: The advantage multiplies its ratio to the old type every generation, so its share grows like compound interest: slow while rare, then fast.
